text: IT Service Management is the discipline of planning, delivering, supporting, and improving the IT services an organization provides. It's not the help desk, not a ticketing tool, and not any single team. Those are implementations of ITSM thinking. An organization can own every enterprise ITSM tool on the market and still have no real ITSM, if nobody has defined what a service is, who owns it, or what "working" even means for it.

Before ITSM takes hold, IT support looks the same everywhere: something breaks, someone notices, someone technical fixes it, and everyone moves on until the next thing breaks. There's no record of how often it recurs, no agreed time limit for fixing it, and no plan beyond calling whoever happens to know that system. That model scales only as far as institutional memory does, and it breaks the moment that one person leaves.

ITSM replaces firefighting with managing. Services get defined owners, agreed performance targets, and documented procedures for common requests and failures, plus a feedback loop that uses what went wrong last time to prevent it next time. The incidents don't disappear — they just stop depending entirely on memory and heroics.

Here's the distinction that trips people up most: the email server is technology. The corporate email service — with an availability target, a support path, onboarding, and a security policy built around it — is the service. ITIL 4 defines a service formally as a means of enabling value co-creation, by facilitating outcomes the customer wants, without the customer having to manage specific costs and risks.

Notice what that definition leaves out — no mention of servers, software versions, or network diagrams. It's defined entirely by the outcome delivered and the costs and risks taken off the customer's plate. Two organizations can run identical technology underneath and still deliver very different services, depending on what's actually built around it.

ITSM is the broad discipline. ITIL is the most widely adopted framework for actually practicing it, now in its fourth major version, and it's the shared vocabulary this entire course will build on. Next up: why organizations go to the trouble of formalizing that practice with a framework in the first place.
